title: Accelerating Dropless MoE Training in JAX with NVIDIA Transformer Engine | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA reports that Transformer Engine plus JAX raises DeepSeek-V3 671B training from an unoptimized 103 TFLOPS/GPU — where inter-GPU communication consumed 84% of accumulated kernel time — to 1,068 TFLOPS/GPU, a 10.4x gain, and sustains 97% scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs on GB300 NVL72. The gains come from making dropless MoE practical at scale: cuBLAS-backed grouped GEMMs for ragged expert shapes, MXFP8 group quantization on Blackwell, and NCCL EP fusing dispatch and combine with token deduplication across NVLink and InfiniBand.

insights.claim: An unoptimized JAX baseline training DeepSeek-V3 on NVIDIA GB200 achieved just 103 TFLOPS/GPU, with inter-GPU communication consuming 84% of accumulated kernel time.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Most of a naive large-MoE cluster's purchased FLOPS are wasted on communication, meaning software, not silicon, is the binding constraint on realized training capacity.
insights.quote: an unoptimized baseline achieved just 103 TFLOPS/GPU with inter-GPU communication consuming 84% of accumulated kernel time
insights.locator: What are the challenges involved in MoE training?

insights.claim: Targeted Transformer Engine and JAX kernel optimizations raised DeepSeek-V3 training throughput to 1,068 TFLOPS/GPU, a 10.4x improvement over the unoptimized baseline.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: A 10x software-only throughput gain on existing hardware is effectively a 10x cut in training cost per token — a material deflationary force on frontier training budgets.
insights.locator: What are the challenges involved in MoE training?

insights.claim: The full stack sustains 97% scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs relative to a 128-GPU baseline when training DeepSeek-V3 671B on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 hardware, with measurements spanning 128 to 2,048 GPUs.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Near-linear multirack scaling for sparse models validates rack-scale NVL72 systems as the unit of frontier training capacity and supports large cluster orders.
insights.quote: The system sustains 97% efficiency at 1,024 GPUs
insights.locator: High multirack scaling performance with JAX

insights.claim: Multirack scaling is where most training systems struggle because communication overhead tends to scale faster than compute, so batch-size and communication inefficiencies that are negligible on a single node compound quickly across thousands of GPUs.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Cluster economics degrade superlinearly without interconnect-aware software, which is the structural reason vertically integrated networking plus software wins large training deals.
insights.quote: Multirack scaling is where most systems struggle, as communication overhead tends to scale faster than compute.
insights.locator: High multirack scaling performance with JAX

themes.theme: Why MoE breaks conventional GPU kernels

insights.claim: Mixture of Experts replaces one dense feed-forward network shared by all tokens with many smaller expert networks plus a learned router selecting Top-K experts, giving efficient training through conditional computation.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Conditional computation decouples parameter count from training FLOPs, which is the mechanism behind cheaper frontier-class models and lower compute per unit of capability.
insights.locator: Mixture of experts (MoE) has become one of the defining architectural trends

insights.claim: DeepSeek, Qwen and Mixtral are cited as MoE models that match or exceed the performance of dense counterparts at a fraction of the training compute, making MoE a defining architectural trend in large-scale training.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: The sparse architecture that open Chinese and European labs standardized on is now NVIDIA's optimization target, confirming MoE as the default frontier training shape.
insights.locator: Mixture of experts (MoE) has become one of the defining architectural trends

insights.claim: Because the router is learned, its expert-preference distribution becomes heavily skewed during training and no two batches produce the same expert loads, so there is no clean rectangular GEMM to batch and dispatch.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Load imbalance is emergent and data-dependent, so MoE efficiency cannot be solved by static planning — it requires runtime-adaptive kernels.
insights.quote: No two batches produce the same expert loads, and within a single batch, one expert might receive many more tokens than another.
insights.locator: What are the challenges involved in MoE training?

insights.claim: Ragged tensors are a fundamental problem because most libraries are highly optimized for uniform, rectangular data structures, leaving MoE-specific bottlenecks — token routing, expert dispatch and gather, all-to-all communication and ragged expert GEMMs — that simply do not exist in dense models.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: The existing dense-optimized software ecosystem is a poor fit for sparse models, creating a durable software moat for whoever ships production ragged-shape kernels.
insights.locator: In MoE, tokens are routed dynamically to different experts

insights.claim: In dropless MoE every token is processed by its selected expert regardless of load imbalance, preserving model quality but placing heavy demands on the system.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Quality-preserving routing is now achievable without the usual throughput penalty, removing a hidden quality tax that capacity-limited training silently pays.
insights.locator: How is dropless MoE different from capacity-based MoE?

insights.claim: Capacity-based MoE assigns each expert a fixed token budget and either trims or pads the overflow, forcing a direct tradeoff where dropping means training on incomplete data and padding means wasted compute and memory.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Names the specific quality-versus-efficiency tradeoff embedded in most existing MoE training runs, a diligence question for any lab claiming MoE parity with dense models.
insights.quote: drop the overflow tokens and the model trains on incomplete data, or pad to avoid dropping and pay the cost in wasted compute and memory
insights.locator: How is dropless MoE different from capacity-based MoE?

insights.claim: The MegaBlocks work made dropless training viable by reformulating expert computation as block-sparse matrix multiplication, which required new block-sparse GPU kernels, optimized grouped GEMM and dispatch/combine primitives built for variable token counts.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Traces the dropless capability to a specific research lineage now productized in vendor libraries — research-to-infrastructure lag of only a few years in this area.
insights.locator: How is dropless MoE different from capacity-based MoE?

insights.claim: Committing to dropless MoE requires kernels that accept dynamic shapes and still work when those shapes are inaccessible on the CPU, so that CUDA graphs remain usable and recompilation is avoided.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: The CPU-visibility constraint is the non-obvious engineering requirement that blocks naive implementations — a real barrier to entry for competing accelerator software stacks.
insights.locator: What specialized optimizations are required for dropless MoE?

insights.claim: Grouped GEMM handles all expert matmuls in a single kernel call using each expert's actual token count, replacing prior approaches that either looped GEMM kernels — requiring latency-incurring Device-to-Host copies of token counts that break CUDA graphs — or used batched GEMMs padded to worst-case capacity.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Removes the two classic MoE inefficiencies at once — host-sync latency and padding waste — which is the single largest source of the reported throughput gain.
insights.locator: Optimization 1: Grouped GEMM

insights.claim: Transformer Engine's grouped_gemm / ragged_dot is backed by cuBLAS and cuBLASLt, mapping onto NVIDIA's best-performing GEMM libraries to deliver full Tensor Core utilization even with irregular expert shapes.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Sparse-model performance is routed through NVIDIA's proprietary CUDA math libraries, deepening rather than loosening the CUDA lock-in for MoE training.
insights.locator: Optimization 1: Grouped GEMM

insights.claim: On NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs the grouped GEMM path opens MXFP8 block scaling for expert matmuls via Transformer Engine grouped quantization kernels, with group-aware MXFP8 quantization listed as a core building block.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Low-precision MXFP8 training is a Blackwell-gated capability, giving a concrete performance reason to upgrade from Hopper-generation fleets for MoE workloads.
insights.locator: Optimization 1: Grouped GEMM

insights.claim: Transformer Engine fuses the Dispatch stage (permuting and sending tokens across GPUs) and the Combine stage (routing results back and accumulating per-expert outputs) into a tightly integrated kernel path, replacing a naive serial chain where the GPU stalls between steps and data is read and written to memory repeatedly.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Communication-compute overlap, not raw FLOPS, is where MoE training efficiency is won or lost at scale.
insights.quote: EP is the counterpart to grouped GEMM: grouped GEMM handles what happens inside each expert; EP handles everything around it.
insights.locator: Optimization 2: Expert parallelism to integrate Dispatch and Combine

insights.claim: NCCL EP is a communication backend tuned specifically for the irregular, imbalanced traffic patterns produced by expert-parallel routing, and it deduplicates tokens so a token dispatched to multiple experts on the same rank or to multiple ranks on a remote InfiniBand node traverses the network only once and is replicated on the receiving node.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Purpose-built MoE collectives conserve scarce interconnect bandwidth, extending NVIDIA's networking advantage into the communication library layer.
insights.locator: Optimization 2: Expert parallelism to integrate Dispatch and Combine

insights.claim: JAX rematerialization APIs let intermediate activations be offloaded to host memory rather than kept on device for the entire forward pass, and in DeepSeek-V3 training the query and value projection results are offloaded to host to save memory.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Host memory becomes an active tier in the training memory hierarchy, easing HBM capacity pressure and raising the value of high-bandwidth CPU-GPU links.
insights.locator: JAX host offloading

insights.claim: XLA by default runs communication on a single stream, serializing collectives that could execute in parallel and exposing some on the critical path; multi-stream collectives let the compiler schedule independent collectives concurrently across separate CUDA streams, overlapping cross-node InfiniBand transfers with intra-node NVLink communication to use both fabrics at once.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Dual-fabric concurrency is a compiler-level unlock that increases effective interconnect utilization without any hardware change.
insights.locator: XLA multistreaming collectives

insights.claim: The Latency Hiding Scheduler decides which collectives are safe to overlap by analyzing replica groups and checking deadlock risk, so memory-bandwidth gains arrive automatically without manual annotation.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Automatic scheduling lowers the expert-engineering barrier to efficient large-scale training, widening the pool of teams that can run frontier-scale jobs.
insights.locator: XLA multistreaming collectives

insights.claim: The 10x gain came from stacking four progressive optimization layers — cuBLAS grouped GEMM, XLA multistream collectives, MXFP8 group quantization, host activation offloading — before finally adding the optimized expert-parallelism implementation.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: No single trick delivers the gain; the multiplicative stack explains why full-stack vendors capture performance leadership that point solutions cannot match.
insights.locator: What is the training performance impact of MoE in JAX with Transformer Engine?

insights.claim: NVIDIA plans to add NVFP4, quantization fused with GEMM, and all-to-all overlap to the Transformer Engine JAX bindings.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: The next precision step down to NVFP4 plus fused quantization signals further training-cost deflation ahead on the same Blackwell-class hardware.
insights.locator: We plan to add NVFP4

insights.claim: The optimizations ship pre-integrated in the NVIDIA NGC MaxText container with Transformer Engine built in, with a specific dated image (ghcr.io/nvidia/jax:maxtext-2026-09-09 or newer) and published configuration flags for exact reproduction of the DeepSeek-V3 671B results.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Publishing a reproducible container and config converts a benchmark claim into an adoptable default, accelerating standardization on NVIDIA's JAX MoE path.
insights.locator: How to get started with dropless MoE training

insights.claim: The recommended validation workflow is to start from the reference configuration, verify correctness on a small MoE model, then scale up while tracking step time, TFLOPS/GPU, MFU, grouped GEMM latency and MoE dispatch/combine latency.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Names the five metrics that actually diagnose MoE training efficiency — the right instrumentation to demand when auditing a customer's cluster utilization.
insights.locator: How to get started with dropless MoE training

insights.claim: The reproduction configuration for DeepSeek-V3 671B uses a 128-GPU layout of expert parallelism 8 combined with total FSDP 16 (ICI 8 × DCN 2), per-device batch size 6, 4,096 max sequence length and capacity_factor 1.0, and the authors caution the tuning is model-specific rather than general.
insights.speaker: Seonghee Lee
insights.so_what: Parallelism layouts remain hand-tuned per model, so headline efficiency numbers do not transfer automatically to a different architecture or cluster shape.
insights.quote: this configuration is specific to DeepSeek-V3; different models will require different tuning
insights.locator: Performance reproduction for DeepSeek V3
